presentingComplaint: Drenching night sweats, 9 kg unintentional weight loss and low-grade evening fevers, incidentally worked up while recovering on the orthopaedic ward after hip surgery.
history: A 73-year-old retired schoolteacher was admitted 6 days ago for dynamic hip screw fixation of a left neck-of-femur fracture sustained in a low-energy fall. He is on chronic polypharmacy - amlodipine, ramipril, metformin, atorvastatin, omeprazole, aspirin (recently switched to prophylactic enoxaparin peri-operatively), tamsulosin and as-required paracetamol/codeine. Post-operatively the nursing staff noted recurrent drenching night sweats requiring linen changes and persistent low-grade evening pyrexia despite a clean wound, negative cultures and no other localising source. On focused review he reports 3-4 months of progressive fatigue, early satiety and roughly 9 kg (approx 12 percent) of unintentional weight loss predating the fall, along with intermittent pruritus. His fall itself may have been precipitated by this general decline. He denies cough, haemoptysis, urinary or bowel symptoms. Ex-smoker (20 pack-years, quit 15 years ago), moderate alcohol, no TB contact, no recent travel.
examination: Cachectic, pale elderly man. Firm, rubbery, non-tender lymphadenopathy palpable in the left cervical, bilateral axillary and left inguinal chains (largest node approx 3 cm, contralateral to surgical site). Spleen palpable 4 cm below the costal margin; liver edge 2 cm, non-tender. Surgical wound clean and dry with no surrounding erythema. Chest clear, no focal consolidation. No jaundice, no petechiae. Mild pedal oedema attributed to immobility.
imaging: CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis: widespread lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm (cervical, mediastinal, para-aortic, iliac) with bulky (>7 cm) para-aortic conglomerate, splenomegaly (17 cm) with focal deposits. No lung mass or cavitation. PET-CT recommended for staging.
microbiology: Blood cultures sterile x2; wound swab and urine culture negative; interferon-gamma release assay negative; HIV, EBV/CMV serology pending; no infective source identified to explain fever and constitutional symptoms.
differentialDiagnoses: Lymphoma (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin) presenting with B-symptoms
Metastatic solid organ malignancy (e.g., lung primary)
finalDiagnosis: Malignancy with B-symptoms - disseminated lymphoma presenting with fever, drenching night sweats and >10% weight loss, incidentally identified in a hospitalised elderly post-operative patient.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Enlargement of Lymph Nodes and Spleen; Malignancies of Lymphoid Cells
ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines - Newly diagnosed and relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma - 2018
NICE Guideline NG12 - Suspected cancer: recognition and referral - 2021
stewardship: Non-infective presentation. Fever and night sweats here are paraneoplastic B-symptoms, not sepsis: cultures are sterile, there is no localising source and the wound is clean. Empirical antibiotics are NOT indicated and should be avoided; reflexive broad-spectrum cover would represent inappropriate antimicrobial use. Priority is excisional lymph node biopsy for histology/immunophenotyping, PET-CT staging, and haemato-oncology referral. Review polypharmacy (renally-cleared and hepatically-metabolised drugs), correct anaemia/hypercalcaemia, and institute tumour-lysis precautions (hydration, monitor urate/potassium) given high LDH and bulky disease before cytotoxic therapy.
contraindications: Avoid empirical antibiotics for paraneoplastic fever without a documented infective source
Avoid corticosteroids before diagnostic biopsy - may transiently shrink lymphoma and obscure histology
Hold nephrotoxic agents and review metformin/ramipril given rising creatinine and tumour-lysis risk
Caution with codeine/opioid accumulation in an elderly patient with reduced renal clearance
edgeCases: Peri-operative inflammatory response and DVT can mimic malignant fever - but sterile cultures, bulky lymphadenopathy and months of preceding weight loss point to malignancy
Disseminated TB can produce identical B-symptoms and splenomegaly; negative IGRA and absence of cavitation lower but do not exclude it - biopsy is decisive
Polypharmacy can cause drug fever; however it does not explain lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly or the elevated LDH
expectedMaiK: Elderly patient with the classic triad of B-symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss) plus painless generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and elevated LDH indicates an underlying lymphoid malignancy; tissue biopsy is required and empirical antibiotics are not.

Any pruritus, bone pain or symptoms of hyperviscosity?
Full drug and dosing review given renal function and polypharmacy?

HIV, EBV serology and TB workup to exclude mimics
